title: Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned by a mutable tag, and those tags hold the production SSH key, the GHCR push token and the code-signing secrets
where: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:195 (webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0), deploy.yml:91,93,100,112,127 (docker/setup-buildx-action@v4, docker/login-action@v4, docker/build-push-action@v7 x3), verify.yml:23,75,137,229 and desktop-release.yml:110 (pnpm/action-setup@v6)
what: `uses:` references resolve a git ref at run time. `v7`, `v6`, `v4`, and `v0.10.0` are all mutable tags in repositories Libriant does not control; the action owner (or anyone who compromises that account or repo) can repoint them at any commit and the next workflow run executes it. There is not one `@<40-hex-sha>` pin in the repository (`grep -rn '@sha256:\|uses: .*@[0-9a-f]\{40\}' .github/` returns nothing). The blast radius is not uniform: `webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0` is handed `secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` — the key that opens a root-equivalent shell on every production host — and the docker/* actions run in a job with `permissions: packages: write` and the GHCR credential the fleet pulls images from.
impact: A single upstream tag repoint (the tj-actions/changed-files pattern, March 2025) yields either the production SSH private key or the ability to push a poisoned `libriant-api:latest` to GHCR that every host pulls on the next deploy. That is total compromise of customer library data, with no signal in the repo.
evidence: READ .github/workflows/deploy.yml:195 `uses: webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0` with `ssh-private-key: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}` at :197. RAN `grep -n "uses:" .github/workflows/*.yml` — 27 occurrences, every external one a tag, zero SHAs. Commit fe0931e ("every GitHub Action to its latest major", 2026-08-22) moved checkout v4->v7, setup-node v4->v7, action-setup v4->v6, build-push v5->v7, login v3->v4, buildx v3->v4, ssh-agent v0.9->v0.10 — i.e. the update pass re-pinned to tags rather than SHAs.
fix: Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, e.g. `uses: webfactory/ssh-agent@a6f90b1f127823b31d4d4a8d96047790581349bd # v0.9.0`. Do this at minimum for webfactory/ssh-agent and the three docker/* actions before deploy.yml is ever dispatched. Add a Dependabot `github-actions` ecosystem entry so SHA bumps arrive as reviewable PRs.

title: Desktop code-signing identity and the auto-update publish token are exposed to a job that executes third-party install scripts and downloads network artifacts
where: .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml:97-208 (job `release`), specifically :118 `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, :123 `pnpm rebuild electron`, :156-191 `electron-builder --publish always`, env block :193-208
what: One job holds, simultaneously: `CSC_LINK` + `CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` (the Apple Developer ID .p12 and its password), `APPLE_API_KEY_P8` (App Store Connect notarization key), the full Azure Trusted Signing service principal (`AZURE_TENANT_ID`/`CLIENT_ID`/`CLIENT_SECRET`), and `GH_TOKEN` with workflow-level `permissions: contents: write` (desktop-release.yml:54-55) on the very repository whose Releases are the electron-updater feed. In that same job it runs `pnpm install`, which executes the install scripts of `@prisma/engines`, `prisma`, `esbuild` and `electron-winstaller` (all allow-listed in pnpm-workspace.yaml:27-40), then `pnpm rebuild electron`, then electron-builder, which downloads the Electron dist archive and (on Windows) 7-Zip from the network at package time. Any one of those packages, or any of the 611 packages installed, running arbitrary Node at install time, can read the signing material out of the environment and can also overwrite the release assets.
impact: Compromise of any package in the install closure -> theft of the Apple Developer ID certificate and the Azure code-signing credential (identity theft that outlives the repo, and cannot be revoked without invalidating every shipped installer), plus the ability to publish a signed installer that every desktop client auto-installs. Fleet-wide RCE on library staff machines from one npm account takeover.
evidence: READ desktop-release.yml:54-55 (`permissions: contents: write`), :117-123 (Install + `pnpm rebuild electron`), :193-208 (all seven signing secrets in one `env:`). RAN an enumeration of every package in node_modules/.pnpm with a preinstall/install/postinstall hook: `@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall=node scripts/postinstall.js`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall=node scripts/preinstall-entry.js`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall=node install.js`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install=node ./script/select-7z-arch.js` — four arbitrary-code hooks that run in this job.
fix: Split the pipeline: build unsigned artifacts in a job with no secrets and `permissions: contents: read`, upload them as workflow artifacts, and sign+publish in a separate minimal job that runs no `pnpm install` (download the artifact, run only the signing tool). Gate the publish job behind an `environment:` with required reviewers. Until then, do not populate MAC_CSC_LINK / AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET.

title: The production API image ships the entire dev and web dependency tree — 611 packages, 880 MB, including eslint, vitest, turbo, typescript, Next.js and Prisma Studio
where: apps/api/Dockerfile:54 (`RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, no --prod) and apps/api/Dockerfile:92 (`COPY --from=build /app /app`); same pattern at apps/web/Dockerfile:24,61
what: The deps stage installs the whole workspace with dev dependencies, and the runtime stage copies /app wholesale. Nothing prunes. The image therefore contains every root devDependency (eslint 10.9.0, typescript-eslint, prettier, turbo, tsx, typescript 6.0.3), the API's own devDependencies (vitest 4.1.11, supertest), the complete Next.js 16 tree (198 MB) including the SWC and lightningcss native binaries, sharp + libvips, and — via the Prisma optional peer (see supply-chain-04) — the Prisma CLI (42 MB), @prisma/studio-core (42 MB, a database-browsing web UI), @prisma/dev, @electric-sql/pglite (23 MB, an embedded WASM Postgres) and mysql2. Only apps/api/src actually runs.
impact: Three concrete harms. (1) Attack surface: a foothold in the API container lands in a ready-made toolkit — a TypeScript compiler, a bundler, a MySQL client and an embedded Postgres, all executable by the `node` user, on a container that already holds CONTROL_DATABASE_URL and every tenant credential. (2) CVE surface: every future advisory in eslint/vitest/turbo/Next.js becomes a production advisory that has to be triaged and shipped, permanently. (3) Cost: ~880 MB of node_modules pulled to each host on every deploy, on a pipeline that already prunes images at deploy.yml:294 to avoid ENOSPC.
evidence: RAN a faithful replay of the API Dockerfile deps stage in a scratch directory (copied exactly the manifests apps/api/Dockerfile:40-50 copies, then `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`): result `Packages: +611`, `du -sh node_modules` = **880M**. Largest entries: next@16.3.2 198.3 MB, @next/swc 84.8 MB, @prisma/client 74.9 MB, @prisma/studio-core 42.2 MB, prisma 41.9 MB, @turbo/darwin-arm64 34.9 MB, typescript 23.6 MB, @electric-sql/pglite 23.2 MB, prettier 9.6 MB. A `--prod` install of only the API-relevant workspaces gives 444 packages / 459 MB — so 167 packages and 421 MB are pure dev tooling that has no business on a production host.
fix: Use `pnpm deploy --filter @libriant/api --prod --legacy /app/out` (or `pnpm install --prod` after the Prisma generate step) in the build stage and copy only the pruned output into the runtime stage. Drop apps/web/package.json from the API Dockerfile's COPY set (apps/api/Dockerfile:42) — the API never imports the web app. Verify with `docker image inspect` that eslint/vitest/turbo/next are gone.

title: autoInstallPeers pulls the Prisma CLI, Prisma Studio, a MySQL driver and an embedded WASM Postgres into the production dependency closure — and with them the one open CVE
where: pnpm-lock.yaml:3-5 (`settings: autoInstallPeers: true`), pnpm-lock.yaml:4673-4678 (`@prisma/client@7.9.1` snapshot lists `prisma` and `typescript` under optionalDependencies)
what: `@prisma/client@7.9.1` declares `prisma` and `typescript` as OPTIONAL peer dependencies (`peerDependenciesMeta: {prisma: {optional: true}, typescript: {optional: true}}`). Because `prisma` is also a devDependency of packages/db-control and packages/db-tenant, pnpm resolves the peer and records it as an optionalDependency of the client snapshot. That means it survives even a `--prod` install: the Prisma CLI (41.9 MB) comes along, and with it @prisma/studio-core (42.2 MB), @prisma/dev, @electric-sql/pglite, mysql2 and effect. @prisma/config (a CLI dependency) is where the tree's single open advisory lives.
impact: Prisma Studio — a full database-browsing UI — and a MySQL client library sit in the production image of a multi-tenant library SaaS. Nothing starts them, so this is surface rather than an open door, but it is 130+ MB of code that will never be exercised, will never be patched deliberately, and is what makes `pnpm audit` non-clean. It also defeats the obvious fix for supply-chain-03: switching the Dockerfile to `--prod` alone does not remove any of it.
evidence: READ node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+client@7.9.1*/node_modules/@prisma/client/package.json — `peerDependencies: {prisma: "*", typescript: ">=5.4.0"}`, both marked optional. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4676-4678 showing them promoted to `optionalDependencies`. RAN a clean `pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile` over only {apps/api, apps/site, packages/db-control, packages/db-tenant, packages/shared}: 444 packages, 459 MB, and `ls node_modules/.pnpm` still shows prisma@7.9.1, @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0, @prisma/dev@0.24.17, @electric-sql/pglite@0.4.3, mysql2@3.15.3.
fix: Set `autoInstallPeers: false` in pnpm-workspace.yaml and re-resolve; the Prisma CLI then only appears where it is a real devDependency, and the runtime image loses ~130 MB and the entire elkjs/mysql2/pglite subtree. Re-run the full gate afterwards — turning it off can surface genuinely missing peers, which is the point.

title: Nothing pinned by digest: base images, the third-party pgbouncer image, and the package manager itself are all resolved from live registries at build/deploy time
what: `grep -rn '@sha256:' infra/ .github/ apps/*/Dockerfile` returns nothing. Every base image is a floating tag. `node:26-alpine`, `caddy:2-alpine`, `postgres:16-alpine` and `redis:8-alpine` all move whenever upstream republishes; `edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.2-p0` is a community image (not an official/verified publisher) that sits in the credential path with POSTGRES_PASSWORD in its environment, and its tag is equally mutable. On the host, deploy.yml:296 runs `docker compose pull`, so whatever the tag points to that minute becomes production.
impact: The deployed stack is not reproducible and not verifiable: two deploys of the same IMAGE_TAG can run different Postgres, Redis, Caddy and pgbouncer binaries. A compromised or hijacked upstream tag (edoburu/pgbouncer is the softest target — a single-maintainer community image handling the database password) lands straight in production with no signal. Compounding it, deploy.yml:294 runs `docker image prune -af --filter until=72h` BEFORE the pull, so the previous base image is gone and a rollback re-pulls the same floating tag rather than restoring what was running.
evidence: RAN `grep -rn "@sha256:" infra/ .github/ apps/*/Dockerfile` — no output. READ the six image lines above. READ deploy.yml:294-296 (prune, then pull).
fix: Pin each base image as `image: postgres:16-alpine@sha256:<digest>` (tag retained for readability) in the Dockerfiles and in docker-compose.prod.yml, and bump digests deliberately. For pgbouncer, either pin the digest or switch to building a thin image from the official Alpine pgbouncer package so the supply chain is one you control.

title: The documented pnpm pin in all three Dockerfiles is inert — corepack downloads pnpm 11.22.0 from the live registry at image-build time instead
where: apps/api/Dockerfile:29-31, apps/web/Dockerfile:9, infra/caddy/Dockerfile:16 (`corepack prepare pnpm@9.15.4 --activate`) vs package.json:5 (`"packageManager": "pnpm@11.22.0"`)
what: Corepack always honours the nearest package.json `packageManager` field; `corepack prepare X --activate` only sets the fallback for projects that declare nothing. So inside every image build, `pnpm install` is pnpm 11.22.0 fetched from https://registry.npmjs.org/pnpm/-/pnpm-11.22.0.tgz at that moment, not the 9.15.4 the Dockerfiles claim to pin. The `packageManager` value carries no `+sha224.<hash>` integrity suffix, so the pin is a version string resolved from the network, and it is the very binary that then executes the allow-listed install scripts during the build. Commit fe0931e bumped `packageManager` to 11.22.0 and removed the `version: 9.15.4` input from pnpm/action-setup in all five CI jobs, but left the three Dockerfile `corepack prepare` lines behind.
impact: Image builds are not hermetic and not offline-capable: a registry outage, an unpublished version, or a compromised pnpm publish breaks or poisons every build. The `COREPACK_HOME=/opt/corepack` warm-cache scheme at apps/api/Dockerfile:28-31 — which docker-compose.prod.yml:176-178 says is the reason the `migrate` one-shot no longer needs `user: root` — is warming the WRONG pnpm version, so the migrate container's corepack cache is cold and it will try to fetch pnpm 11 into the `node` user's HOME on first run, which is exactly the failure that `user: root` was originally there to avoid.
evidence: RAN with a fresh empty COREPACK_HOME and network disabled, from the repo root: `corepack prepare pnpm@9.15.4 --activate` then `corepack pnpm -v` -> `Network access disabled by the environment; can't reach https://registry.npmjs.org/pnpm/-/pnpm-11.22.0.tgz` — corepack ignored the freshly-prepared 9.15.4 and demanded 11.22.0. Also `/opt/homebrew/bin/pnpm -v` = 9.15.4 but `corepack pnpm -v` = 11.22.0 in this repo, and node_modules/.modules.yaml records `"packageManager": "pnpm@11.22.0"`.
fix: Change the three Dockerfiles to `corepack prepare pnpm@11.22.0 --activate` (or better, `corepack install --global pnpm@11.22.0`) so the pin matches package.json and the cache is warmed for the version that actually runs. Add the integrity hash to `packageManager` (`pnpm@11.22.0+sha224.<hash>`) so corepack verifies the tarball. Then re-test the migrate one-shot as the `node` user offline.

title: Caddy runs as root, holds the Cloudflare origin private key and the ACME account key, and the compose file states the opposite
where: infra/caddy/Dockerfile (no USER directive anywhere), infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:113-163 (caddy service: no `user:`, no `cap_drop`, no `security_opt`), and the contradicting comment at docker-compose.prod.yml:176-179
what: The edge image is `FROM caddy:2-alpine` with nothing after it but a COPY; the official Caddy image sets no USER, so PID 1 in that container is uid 0. Compose adds no `user:`, no `cap_drop: [ALL]` + `cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]`, and no `no-new-privileges`. It is also the container that binds host 80/443/443udp (:135-138), mounts the Cloudflare Origin Certificate private key at `/etc/caddy/origin:ro` (:148), and owns the `caddy_data` volume holding the ACME account key. Meanwhile the comment at :176-179 asserts that removing `user: root` from the `migrate` one-shot "eliminates the only root container in the prod stack" — which is false.
impact: Any Caddy RCE (or a compromised base-image tag, see supply-chain-05) is root inside a container with the TLS origin private key, host ports 80/443, and reachability to both the `edge` and `app` networks. The false comment means the next person reading the stack for a security review will conclude root has already been dealt with and look no further.
evidence: RAN `grep -n USER infra/caddy/Dockerfile apps/api/Dockerfile apps/web/Dockerfile` -> only apps/web/Dockerfile:64 and apps/api/Dockerfile:97 match; the caddy image has none. READ docker-compose.prod.yml:113-163 — no `user:`/`cap_*`/`security_opt` key on the caddy service. Independent proof of uid 0: the container binds :80 and :443 with no `cap_add`, which is only possible as root under the default capability set.
fix: Either run Caddy as a non-root user with `cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]` and `cap_drop: [ALL]`, or accept root and correct the comment at docker-compose.prod.yml:178. In both cases add `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]` to every service and make the origin-key mount `:ro` readable only by the running uid.

title: There is no vulnerability gate anywhere in the pipeline — no pnpm audit, no Dependabot/Renovate, no image scan, no SBOM — and the tree already fails one
where: .github/workflows/verify.yml (four jobs: static-checks, unit-tests, integration-tests, db-migration — none audits dependencies); .github/ contains only `workflows/` (no dependabot.yml, no CODEOWNERS, no SECURITY.md); no renovate.json at the repo root
what: The verify gate runs typecheck, lint, prettier, translations, assets, unit, integration, migrations and the DR drill — and zero supply-chain checks. Nothing in CI runs `pnpm audit`. Nothing scans the built images. Nothing produces an SBOM. And because every install site uses `--frozen-lockfile`, the resolved versions are frozen forever: without Dependabot or Renovate no mechanism exists that will ever raise a dependency version again. The 2026-06-14 audit already recorded this exact gap (docs/audit/production-readiness-findings-2026-06-14.json:2172 recommends adding `pnpm audit --prod` or Dependabot) and it was not acted on.
impact: The day a Next.js, NestJS, Prisma or ioredis advisory lands, nobody here finds out. For a product holding Greek public libraries' member records under GDPR, 'we had no process for learning about known vulnerabilities' is the finding an incident review writes down. The gap is not theoretical: `pnpm audit` fails today (see supply-chain-09).
evidence: RAN `grep -rn 'pnpm audit|npm audit|trivy|grype|snyk|osv-scanner|sbom|cyclonedx'` across the repo excluding node_modules — the only matches are inside docs/audit/ (the June audit's own scripts and its unactioned recommendation). RAN `ls -a .github/` -> `workflows` only. RAN `pnpm audit --json` -> 1 high, 0 critical over 895 dependencies.
fix: Add a `supply-chain` job to verify.yml running `pnpm audit --prod --audit-level=high` (it will fail on supply-chain-09 until Prisma ships a fix, so start with `--audit-level=critical` plus a non-blocking full report). Add .github/dependabot.yml with `npm` (grouped, weekly), `github-actions` and `docker` ecosystems. Generate a CycloneDX SBOM in the build job and attach it to the image.

title: One open advisory in the tree: deepmerge-ts 7.1.5 (CVE-2026-40345, rated high) via the Prisma CLI — not reachable from request handling, but it blocks any audit gate
where: node_modules path `@prisma/client@7.9.1 > prisma@7.9.1 > @prisma/config@7.9.1 > deepmerge-ts@7.1.5`; pnpm-lock.yaml:4680-4684 (`@prisma/config@7.9.1` dependencies include `deepmerge-ts: 7.1.5`)
what: GHSA-ggr8-5vv4-36mx / CVE-2026-40345, CWE-674 stack exhaustion when merging recursive object graphs. Vulnerable `<8.0.0`, patched `>=8.0.0`; the tree has 7.1.5 and there is no route to 8.x without a Prisma release, because @prisma/config pins it. Reachability assessed rather than assumed: deepmerge-ts is used by @prisma/config to merge prisma.config layers, which runs only under the Prisma CLI (`prisma generate` at image build, `prisma migrate deploy` in the `migrate` one-shot). The inputs are the repo's own config files, not tenant or request data. The API's request path never loads @prisma/config.
impact: Real exploitability against Libriant: negligible — an attacker would need to control the Prisma config file, at which point they already control the build. The operational impact is different and real: this advisory is why `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` cannot be turned on as a blocking gate (supply-chain-08) without an ignore entry, and an ignore entry added on day one tends to become permanent.
evidence: RAN `pnpm audit --json`: `{"vulnerabilities":{"info":0,"low":0,"moderate":0,"high":1,"critical":0},"totalDependencies":895}`, sole advisory `deepmerge-ts <8.0.0 -> >=8.0.0`, six paths all rooted at prisma@7.9.1. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4680-4684 confirming @prisma/config@7.9.1 -> deepmerge-ts 7.1.5 with no override available (an override to ^8 would break @prisma/config's expected API).
fix: Do not force an override. Record the reachability assessment above in the repo, set the CI audit gate to `--audit-level=critical` with a full non-blocking `pnpm audit --prod` report, and add a tracked item to re-run the audit on the next Prisma minor. Fixing supply-chain-04 (autoInstallPeers) removes this path from the production image entirely, leaving it dev-only.

title: The production deploy's SSH target list is produced by an unpinned PyPI install whose failure is swallowed
what: `python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml || true` installs the latest PyYAML from PyPI, unpinned and unhashed, on the runner. The python one-liner that follows parses infra/deploy/fleet.yml and writes `hosts=<json>` to $GITHUB_OUTPUT; that JSON becomes the `deploy` job's matrix, and `matrix.host.user` / `matrix.host.ssh` are interpolated directly into the `ssh` command lines at deploy.yml:232, 264, 347 and 399. The `|| true` means a failed or hijacked install is not surfaced here; the script either dies with an opaque ImportError or runs against whatever got installed.
impact: A compromised PyYAML release runs arbitrary code on the runner that immediately afterwards loads the production SSH key, and can rewrite the host matrix. Host-key pinning (deploy.yml:199-221) blocks redirection to an unknown host, but not code execution on the runner, and not deletion or duplication of legitimate hosts. Separately, `|| true` on a step whose output gates production is the wrong failure mode.
evidence: READ deploy.yml:161 `python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml || true` and :162-166 emitting `hosts=` consumed at :189 `matrix: host: ${{ fromJson(needs.plan.outputs.hosts) }}`. RAN `grep -rnE 'curl .*\| *(ba)?sh|pip install|apt-get install' scripts/ infra/ .github/` — this and verify.yml:346 (`apt-get install postgresql-client-16`, a distro package on a throwaway CI runner) are the only two remote-install sites.
fix: Drop the pip install: parse fleet.yml with `yq` (preinstalled on GitHub runners) or convert infra/deploy/fleet.yml to JSON and read it with `jq`. If Python is kept, use `pip install --require-hashes -r` a pinned requirements file, and remove the `|| true`.

title: Any push touching apps/desktop/** publishes a live release to the auto-update feed with no approval gate, on a repository the code admits has no required status checks
where: .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml:27-31 (push trigger), :54-55 (`permissions: contents: write`), :214-225 (job `publish`, no `environment:`), vs .github/workflows/deploy.yml:50-51 ("Required status checks aren't available on this GitHub plan")
what: desktop-release.yml fires on every push to main under apps/desktop/**, builds three installers, and job `publish` runs `gh release edit "$TAG" --draft=false --latest`, which is what electron-updater reads as the update feed. There is no `environment:` on `version`, `release` or `publish`, so no reviewer is ever required. deploy.yml's own comment establishes that this repository has no branch protection and no required status checks — meaning main is directly pushable and the verify gate is enforced only by workflow ordering, not by the platform. There is no CODEOWNERS file.
impact: A single compromised push (or a force-push to main) ships an installer to the desktop fleet, automatically, with no human in the loop. Today the blast radius is bounded because builds are unsigned and the workflow bakes `libriantAutoUpdate=false` (:157, :188) so clients do not silently self-update — that mitigation is good and load-bearing. The moment MAC_CSC_LINK or the Azure secrets are populated, that guard disappears by design and the path becomes push -> signed auto-update -> code execution on every staff machine.
evidence: READ desktop-release.yml:27-31, :54-55, :214-225 — no `environment:` key anywhere in the file (`grep -n 'environment:' .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml` -> no match; deploy.yml:190 has one, desktop-release.yml does not). READ deploy.yml:50-51 for the admission that required status checks are unavailable on this plan.
fix: Add `environment: desktop-release` with a required reviewer to the `publish` job (and to `release` once signing secrets exist). Add a CODEOWNERS file. If required status checks genuinely are unavailable on the current plan, that is a reason to change the plan before shipping signed binaries, not a reason to proceed.

title: Two production dependencies carry no licence at all, and three carry non-permissive or dual licences that need a recorded decision
where: exceljs@4.4.0 (apps/api/package.json:26) -> unzipper@0.10.14 -> binary@0.3.0 -> buffers@0.1.1 (no `license` field); prisma@7.9.1 -> mysql2@3.15.3 -> seq-queue@0.0.5 (no `license` field); next@16.3.2 -> sharp@0.35.3 -> @img/sharp-libvips-*@1.3.2 (LGPL-3.0-or-later); @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0 -> elkjs@0.11.1 (EPL-2.0); exceljs@4.4.0 -> jszip@3.10.1 ((MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later))
what: I walked the production closure from every workspace's `dependencies` (496 packages) and read each package.json licence field. The distribution is overwhelmingly clean — 350 MIT, 42 Apache-2.0, 40 ISC, 9 BSD-3-Clause — and critically there is NO AGPL, NO SSPL and NO GPL-only package anywhere in the runtime tree, so there is no copyleft threat to the closed-source product. Five items are not clean: `buffers@0.1.1` and `seq-queue@0.0.5` declare no licence whatsoever (default copyright applies — no grant to use, copy or redistribute); `@img/sharp-libvips-darwin-arm64@1.3.2` and its siblings are LGPL-3.0-or-later native libraries; `elkjs@0.11.1` is EPL-2.0 (file-level weak copyleft); `jszip@3.10.1` is a dual `(MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later)` where the MIT election must be recorded. There is no LICENSE, NOTICE or third-party-attribution file anywhere in the repository, and the desktop installers — which ARE distributed to users — ship MIT/Apache/BSD code with no accompanying notices, which those licences require.
impact: The two unlicensed packages are the sharp end: strictly, Libriant has no grant to copy or distribute them, and one of them arrives through exceljs, a first-order runtime dependency used by the customer-facing export feature. In practice this is a due-diligence problem rather than a Monday outage — it is what a customer's procurement review, an acquirer, or a Greek public-sector tender questionnaire asks for and Libriant cannot currently answer. LGPL-3.0 (libvips) imposes no source obligation for SaaS, but does if sharp is ever bundled into the distributed desktop app. EPL-2.0 (elkjs) is only present because Prisma Studio is in the tree (see supply-chain-04) and vanishes with it.
evidence: RAN a script that resolved the 496-package production closure from pnpm-lock.yaml importers+snapshots and read every package.json `license`: 350 MIT / 42 Apache-2.0 / 40 ISC / 9 BSD-3-Clause / 3 Unlicense / 2 UNKNOWN / 2 MIT-X11 / 2 BlueOak-1.0.0 / 1 each LGPL-3.0-or-later, CC-BY-4.0, BSD-2-Clause, EPL-2.0, (MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later), MIT-0, (MIT AND Zlib), 0BSD. RAN a parent trace: `buffers@0.1.1 <- binary@0.3.0 <- unzipper@0.10.14 <- exceljs@4.4.0 <- ROOT:apps/api`; `seq-queue@0.0.5 <- mysql2@3.15.3 <- prisma@7.9.1`; `elkjs@0.11.1 <- @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0`. RAN `ls` at the repo root — no LICENSE or NOTICE file.
fix: Record a licence policy and generate a third-party notices file (`pnpm licenses list --prod --json` into a NOTICE.md) shipped inside the desktop installers and linked from the app's About page. For buffers/seq-queue: fixing supply-chain-04 removes seq-queue outright; for buffers, either accept the risk in writing or replace exceljs's unzipper path (exceljs is only used for import/export). Record the MIT election for jszip. Confirm sharp/libvips is never bundled into the Electron app.

title: The allowBuilds allowlist is correct and complete, but two of its five entries are misdescribed and the release workflow contains an allowlist bypass
what: Good news first, verified rather than assumed: I enumerated every package in node_modules/.pnpm carrying a preinstall/install/postinstall hook. Exactly five registry packages have one — @prisma/engines (postinstall), prisma (preinstall), esbuild (postinstall), electron-winstaller (install), msgpackr-extract (install) — and all five are explicitly decided in allowBuilds. Nothing is silently blocked, nothing is blanket-approved. Two defects sit on top of that. (1) desktop-release.yml:123 runs `pnpm rebuild electron` with the comment "pnpm blocks Electron's large binary postinstall by default" — electron@43.4.1 has NO `scripts` field at all, so the step executes nothing and the comment is false; the Electron dist is actually downloaded by electron-builder at package time. `pnpm rebuild <pkg>` is nonetheless a general primitive for running a build script the allowlist deliberately withheld, sitting in the workflow that holds the code-signing secrets (supply-chain-02). (2) `prepare` scripts (bullmq, undici, uuid, cron-parser and ~60 others carry them) are not covered by allowBuilds — harmless for registry tarballs, which never run `prepare`, but it means the allowlist is not the complete story if a dependency is ever pinned to a git URL.
impact: Low on its own. The value at risk is the policy's credibility: pnpm-workspace.yaml:24-26 states the rule is to decide each install script individually, and a `pnpm rebuild` in CI is an unreviewed exception to it. The false comment also means the next person will not notice the step is dead and can be deleted.
evidence: RAN a walk of every package.json under node_modules/.pnpm reporting preinstall/install/postinstall/prepare: only `@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install`, `msgpackr-extract@3.0.4 install` among install-time hooks. RAN `python3 -c "json.load(...)['scripts']"` on node_modules/.pnpm/electron@43.4.1_*/node_modules/electron/package.json -> `None`; the package's key list is [author, bin, dependencies, description, engines, files, keywords, license, main, name, repository, types, version] — no `scripts` at all, though a standalone install.js is still shipped. Control: msgpackr-extract (a BLOCKED package) still shows its `install` script, proving pnpm does not strip scripts and the electron result is genuine.
fix: Delete the `pnpm rebuild electron` step (desktop-release.yml:120-123) — it is a no-op — and confirm electron-builder still packages. If a future Electron reintroduces a postinstall, add `electron: true` to allowBuilds with a written justification rather than reaching for `pnpm rebuild`.

title: Two of the eleven pinned overrides apply to packages that are not in the tree, and two more sit below the direct dependency they claim to floor
what: The overrides block is introduced as "Security/compat floors for transitive dependencies" (pnpm-workspace.yaml:8). `hono` and `@hono/node-server` resolve to nothing — `grep -nE '^  hono@|^  @hono/node-server@' pnpm-lock.yaml` returns no match, and they are absent from the lockfile's own `overrides:` effect on resolution. They are leftovers from the Cloudflare Worker that commit 92d8587 deleted ("delete the Cloudflare Worker, drop Turnstile"). Separately, `react`/`react-dom` are floored at ^19.2.6 while apps/web/package.json:11-12 declares ^19.2.8 directly, so those two entries can never bind. The remaining seven (ioredis 6.0.0, multer 2.2.0, uuid 11.1.1, qs 6.15.3, form-data 4.0.6, postcss 8.5.26, esbuild 0.28.2) are all live and all resolve at or above their floor.
impact: No current exposure — these are dead entries, not wrong ones. The harm is that a security-floor list containing entries that provably bind to nothing is a list nobody has verified, which is how a genuinely stale floor survives the next review. A caret floor also cannot mask a fix (it only raises), so there is no hidden downgrade here; the one real risk in this pattern is a future advisory whose fix requires a MAJOR bump (e.g. form-data 5.x), which the `^4.0.6` override would then pin the whole tree away from.
evidence: RAN `for p in ioredis react react-dom multer uuid qs form-data postcss esbuild hono @hono/node-server; do grep -nE "^  $p@" pnpm-lock.yaml; done` — every package resolves except `hono` and `@hono/node-server`, which produce no output. Resolved versions read from pnpm-lock.yaml: ioredis@6.0.0, react@19.2.8, react-dom@19.2.8, multer@2.2.0, uuid@11.1.1, qs@6.15.3, form-data@4.0.6, postcss@8.5.26, esbuild@0.28.2. I also checked the one override with real API-break potential: `uuid: ^11.1.1` is forced onto exceljs@4.4.0, which declares `uuid: ^8.3.0` — exceljs uses `const {v4: uuidv4} = require('uuid')` (lib/xlsx/xform/sheet/cf-ext/cf-rule-ext-xform.js:1), and uuid@11's CJS entry still exports a named `v4`, so this specific forced upgrade is safe.
fix: Delete the `hono` and `@hono/node-server` overrides and the two react floors, leaving only the seven that bind. Add a one-line comment per remaining override naming the advisory or compat reason it exists, so the next review can retire them by evidence instead of by guess.

title: What is actually sound in the supply chain — verified, so the next reviewer does not re-derive it
what: Four things I checked and found correct. (1) Every resolution in pnpm-lock.yaml carries a sha512 `integrity` hash, and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` reproduces the tree byte-for-byte from the content-addressable store — I replayed it and got `Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped`. (2) pnpm 11 enforces a minimum-release-age supply-chain policy by default and it is active: the install printed `✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 15h ago)`, and commit fe0931e records that it rejected the lockfile over two transitives published within the previous few hours — that is a real defence against the compromised-package publish window, and it is on. (3) A fork pull request cannot publish or deploy: ci.yml triggers on `pull_request` (never `pull_request_target`), calls verify.yml with no `secrets:` clause, and verify.yml declares `permissions: contents: read` with every job using inline test-only values — so no job in the PR path references a secret at all. (4) The three Dockerfile deps stages omit apps/desktop/package.json while pnpm-workspace.yaml globs `apps/*`; I verified pnpm 11 tolerates the missing importer under `--frozen-lockfile` rather than failing, so the image builds are not broken by that omission.
impact: None — recorded so that these are not re-audited, and so that the pnpm 11 release-age gate is understood as a deliberate defence rather than removed the first time it blocks a build (the fe0931e commit message already flags the temptation).
evidence: RAN in a scratch directory replicating apps/api/Dockerfile:40-50 exactly: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` -> `Scope: all 9 workspace projects / ✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 15h ago) / Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped / Packages: +611 / Done in 3.5s using pnpm v11.22.0` (note: 9 projects found, apps/desktop absent, no error). READ ci.yml:6-19 and verify.yml:10-16 for the trigger and permissions. RAN `grep -rn pull_request_target .github/` -> no match.
fix: No change. Do not add `minimumReleaseAge: 0` or otherwise disable pnpm's supply-chain policy when it blocks a build; wait it out or pin the specific transitive.
